I came across a post on self-improvement from the chans this morning, and it has had me thinking all morning. (See Here) Don't get me wrong, there is something particularly cringey about it - I think it was the self-indulgent, peak-high-school photo that was attached. However, I believe there is a great deal of truth in the post's message, and at the same time, I believe 90% of the readers missed it.

When did it become common for men to start thinking about self-improvement? There is a crucial distinction to make about this. I'm asking about the moment that self-improvement became a conscious activity, a question young men started asking themselves, in which they situate their own self-representation mentally against some process of improving it, further against some vague cultural ideal. What is that ideal? What's informing that ideal? Furthermore, when did improving oneself become such a rational and psychological affair, generally taking place after one has first found themselves wanting, and finding such a rich and dense body of "knowledge" on how to do just that: IMPROVE.

I think what we are dealing with is a generation of beached explorers, abandoned men; men abandoned by the generation of fathers before them, marooned in a culture, which itself is the antithesis of their development as naturally good men, as competitors, as winners. Self-improvement has stepped in as the consumer solution for fatherhood, for the entire milieu of a home life featuring a mother and father, as if that vital function and experience could be distilled into e-books and email newsletters.

That post contained a particular statement that I haven't been able to shake:

"...you don't ever find yourself one night lying in bed alone wondering why..."

This is the real insight. Men who are caught up living aren't occupied in their thoughts at night about some vague cultural ideal of manhood, anxiously estimating how they fall short of it, how they're lonely and should try to improve, moving toward that ideal so they can get the things they want. More importantly, a genuinely successful male's thoughts aren't extricated from a story. The "winners" of society, their thoughts, are always embodied in a story, enmeshed in an environment with people and a narrative. Typically, they are always about overcoming some other male. A "winner" doesn't live like a search algorithm for how to "do this like a true alpha", constantly making plans and schedules for a self-improvement routine, posting pictures of his ideal self on fucking corkboard and marking days off on the calendar before he can start his plan.

He's just being competitive. He is overcome and moved in his life by trying to do something better than someone else. Not a vague "someone else", not some cultural comic book story, but a real person. A healthy male grows up learning to deal with real adversaries, to build his own support structure through camaraderie with other males, but always living in an actual story and actively trying to beat someone. That someone has a name, and a face, they've met, the challenges are real. That is, the game is real, not the foggy mental image of chasing self-improvement, but legitimate improvement that comes about from needing to overcome someone else. Self-overcoming, while not impossible, seems to me to be inferior, and I think it has the potential to lead men astray. Nothing motivates a man to change than defeat, loss, and the need to win. To never feel the shame of actual defeat, from an enemy with a face.

Successful men aren't awake at night wondering why, oh why the world hasn't given them this. Deciding it's because of this or that defect in them as a male, and wondering what system they can go about undertaking to improve themselves. These men, usually from a young age, have always been put in situations with clear enemies, clear rules, and told: "Go fucking win. Figure it out. That's what you have a coach for, that's why you have teammates. Figure it out, and don't whine if you don't." I find it terribly interesting how much of athletics culture finds it's way into self-improvement. This is very, very telling about exactly what is missing for us psychologically. For fuck's sake, these people call themselves coaches. I think the entire problem is we're missing the root, the real dirt of culture that actually causes us to improve.

The key insight, for me, is exactly what's implicit in the self-improvement culture and what it suggests is missing. They call themselves coaches, and frame this as if you have competition with yourself. You're here to beat you. Again, no winners lay awake at night thinking about beating themselves. They're thinking about their enemies and the game.

But as men, we are being raised inside of a culture that discourages competition. I don't even mean to indicate here the really gross forms of this. I'm more interested in the subtler anti-competitive aspects of culture: the rugged individualism, the "you do you" and let everyone else be, don't criticize this or that, everyone is equal, we're all trying to improve, we all find our own path.

No, we don't. The reason certain people seem to do things right, and life works out for them like that post suggested, is because they were operating according to a formula. A formula that came from exposure to a father. A father with a truth theory about the world, which transmitted to the son very black-and-white statements of value, about right and wrong. There was no him-hawing, i.e. "this person thinks this, and that's okay." No. It's: "this is how you do it." Whether it's the case that the father was absolutely right is not what's at issue. It's that the father was there and doing this. A man raised in this environment has standards for himself, and he must call things right and wrong. He can only think in those terms. It motivates his Being. He looks at his world and implicitly thinks, "He is doing this wrong. I'm going to do it right. I'm going to do it better because I have the truth." And the way he has been raised to do this is via competition.

Consider what all of this suggests about the larger human social organism. We discover truth by competing. None of the psychology I just described arises in a milieu consisting of: "Don't criticize. Let everyone be themselves. Worry about yourself. Don't criticize other people. We're all getting there in our own way." Man doesn't thrive like this. He suffers in this sort of space. Effectively, it is removing the quiet voice of his father, and his father, and his grandfather's father going back (Lo there do I see the line of my people). It cuts this voice off, and it says to the young man, "Your father wasn't right. Your father had opinions. But everyone else's father is just as right as yours was." Also, "I'm divorcing your dad. We'll get you some self-improvement books to replace him when you're 15."

This culture we are living in is the culture of single motherhood. I don't mean that it is a culture that features a lot of single motherhood. I mean that as a culture, it is single motherhood. This culture we are living in is a diffuse, unfocused amplification of the mother, because she too is missing the male. She is like a receptacle without a plug to channel her energy into an appliance, i.e. something productive. Culture has lost the Father.

And so there is a race of men, all self-improving. We do it like its masturbation. What are we chasing? Who knows. Nothing is right or true. You do you. Do whatever motivates you. Watch this Youtuber. Try to be like the guy from that HBO show, figure out how to apply that in your life. We're all reading books and watching motivational Youtube videos, but we don't have the story. We aren't living our lives with a discrete, real enemy with a name. We've been discouraged from that. We all want the highest ideal, the peak of perfection, and we're chasing it in the clouds, instead of finding it closer to home, right in front of us, the enemy with a fucking name. Instead, we've made ourselves the enemy. We're in a battle with us. And that battle must be solo. Mom said so. Teacher said so. Groups of men are bad. Nobody else is wrong, we're just intolerant. Nobody else is wrong, you're just a hater. Don't tell anyone they're wrong, just do you. Improve yourself. GO WORK ON YOURSELF. CLEAN YOUR ROOM.

Sometimes the self-improvement works to motivate us for a little while, but ultimately it's poor psychology. We shouldn't be pursuing improvement by defeating ourselves, rather, we should be trying to defeat an enemy. Improve from the sort of psychology that says, "You're wrong. I'm going to do it better. I'm going to show you that I do it better." Nor should we be seeking improvement, in my opinion, by pursuing some female-determined cultural ideal, but instead, we should be focused on the game. Our improvement should derive naturally from trying to fucking beat our enemy. I think the "winners" in society have classically been the men that weren't awake at night wondering how be more like this guy. No, the "winners" have been the men wondering what their own fathers would have to say to them, and picturing the face of the adversary that they live to go defeat.

Everything inside of us, Lo do I see my Father, wants to fucking say, "That's wrong. You're wrong." We need to take back the right to do this. It belongs to man. The mother won't say this. She would let what's yours be taken, including your truth, if it meant feeding more mouths. We're being told that the vital function of men in society, our very Being, is outmoded on account of the fact that social values are changing. They're changing because we aren't saying "No".
